title: Wire Fraud in Real Estate: What Agents Should Tell Buyers
description: Real estate fraud cost victims over $275 million in 2025. Here's what agents should tell buyers about red flags, verification, and what to do if it happens.
keywords: real estate wire fraud prevention for agents
Southern California real estate wire fraud
image_alt: A man in a grey button-down shirt checks his phone at a desk across from an open laptop

faq.q: How do real estate wire fraud scams work?
faq.a: Criminals gain access to an email account in the transaction or study public listing data, then send convincing fake wiring instructions near closing so the buyer sends funds to an account they control.

faq.q: What should a buyer do before wiring closing funds?
faq.a: Call the escrow or title company at a phone number confirmed independently at the start of the transaction, not one from an email, and verify the account details out loud before sending.

faq.q: What should I do if my buyer wired money to a scammer?
faq.a: Have the buyer call their bank right away to request a wire recall, file a complaint at ic3.gov, and notify escrow, the agents and the lender. Acting quickly can improve the odds of recovery.

body_html:
Your buyer is three days from closing. Loan docs are signed, the appraisal is in, and everyone is relaxed. Then an email lands in their inbox that looks like it came from escrow: "Updated wiring instructions attached. Please send your funds today to avoid delaying closing." Same logo, same signature block, a sender address that's one letter off. That single email is the most dangerous moment in the entire transaction.

Wire fraud isn't a new problem, but it hasn't gone away either, and it's getting harder to spot. As the agent, you're often the person your buyer trusts most and talks to most often. That makes you the best-positioned person to stop it before it starts. Here's what I'd want every agent I work with to tell every buyer, and when to say it.

Why Real Estate Wire Fraud Still Matters

According to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center 2025 report, as summarized by the National Association of REALTORS®, real estate-related fraud cost victims more than $275 million in 2025, reported by at least 12,368 victims. That was up from 9,359 complaints and more than $173 million in losses in 2024. The same report points to artificial intelligence helping scammers appear more convincing and making their schemes harder to detect.

Those figures only count what people reported. And the impact on a single buyer can be devastating: closing funds often represent years of savings, gift money from family, or proceeds from selling a previous home. Once a wire goes out, recovering it gets harder by the hour.

The scheme itself is usually simple. A criminal gains access to an email account somewhere in the transaction (an agent's, a buyer's, an escrow officer's) or simply studies public listing data, then waits. When the timing is right, they send convincing wiring instructions that route the money to an account they control.

The Red Flags Buyers Should Know by Heart

Scam emails tend to share a few traits. Give your buyers this list early and repeat it near closing:

  • "Updated" or "changed" wiring instructions. Legitimate escrow and title companies rarely change wiring instructions mid-transaction. Any change should be treated as suspicious until verified.
  • Urgency and pressure. "Wire today or you'll lose the house" is a classic tactic. Real escrow timelines can almost always absorb a verification phone call.
  • Look-alike email addresses. One swapped letter, an extra word, or a different domain ending. On a phone screen, these are easy to miss.
  • Requests to keep it quiet. Any message that says not to call or not to involve the agent is a warning sign by itself.
  • New phone numbers in the email. Scammers include their own number so the "verification" call goes straight to them.
  • Unusual payment methods. Requests for gift cards, cryptocurrency, or payment apps for closing funds should stop everything.

A Simple Wire Safety Script for Agents

The most effective protection is a conversation that happens before any money moves. I'd suggest building it into your process at three points:

  1. At the buyer consultation. Tell buyers plainly: "No one on our team will ever email you new wiring instructions. If you get one, call me before you do anything." Hearing it early makes it stick.
  2. When escrow opens. Share the escrow officer's name and a phone number you've confirmed independently, so the buyer has a trusted number that didn't come from an email. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau recommends identifying trusted contacts, such as the agent and settlement agent, and confirming the closing process and payment instructions with them in person or by phone. Some teams agree on a code phrase too.
  3. A few days before funds are due. Send a short reminder by text or phone: "Before you wire, call escrow at the number we gave you and confirm the account details out loud." This is exactly when fraudulent emails tend to arrive.

Keep the tone calm. You're not trying to scare anyone. You're giving them a habit, the same way you'd tell them not to open new credit during escrow. (If you want a companion handout, my post on things not to do while your loan is in escrow covers the other common mistakes.)

Verification Habits That Actually Work

Here's how the safe approach compares to what scammers count on:

Risky habitSafer habit
Calling the number in the emailCalling a number confirmed at the start of escrow or from the company's official website
Replying to the email to ask if it's realStarting a new phone call, never a reply thread
Wiring the full amount on the last dayBuilding in time to verify, and confirming receipt with escrow right after sending
Emailing bank details or account numbersSharing sensitive information only through secure portals or by phone with verified contacts
Clicking links or attachments to "view" instructionsGetting instructions through the escrow company's established secure process

Agents can protect themselves too. Turn on multi-factor authentication for your email and transaction platforms, use strong unique passwords, and avoid sending wiring details yourself. If you never forward wire instructions, your buyers learn that any instructions from "you" are fake. That's a powerful default.

Your loan officer is part of this, too. On my files, the lending side never sends a buyer wiring instructions for closing funds, and we reinforce the same message your buyer hears from you. Consistency across the team is what makes the warning believable.

What to Do If a Buyer Wires to the Wrong Account

Speed matters more than anything else. If a buyer suspects they've sent money to a fraudster, they should:

  • Call their bank immediately and ask for a wire recall. The CFPB notes that reporting as soon as possible can increase the chances of recovering funds.
  • File a complaint with the FBI at ic3.gov. The NAR article describes a case in which a closing-related wire of more than $449,000 was frozen through the IC3's Recovery Asset Team after a quick report.
  • Notify escrow, the agents, and the lender right away so everyone can protect the transaction and adjust the timeline if needed.
  • Preserve everything: the emails, headers, phone numbers, and wire confirmation.

As the agent, your job in that moment is to keep the buyer moving quickly and to loop in the right people. Have the bank's fraud line and the IC3 site ready to share. Questions about liability or what to do legally should go to an attorney. And because a fraud incident can push back closing, it helps to know why escrows get delayed and how to manage it before you need to.

The Takeaway

Wire fraud depends on one thing: a buyer acting on an email without picking up the phone. You can break that chain with a few repeated sentences at the right moments. Tell buyers early that instructions won't change by email, give them a verified escrow number, remind them right before funds are due, and make sure they know to act fast if something goes wrong.

It's a small investment of time that protects your client's savings, your closing, and your reputation.
